newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 21.

text.p: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- M&S SEES ONE BILLION STG PROFIT BUT FAILS TO DISPEL FEARS

Marks and Spencer have announced one billion stg profits for last year for the first time. However, shares dropped as investors grew concerned about higher costs, a weaker than expected performance from food and the impact of a strong pound, which will cost 20 million stg this year. Richard Greenbury, chairman, said the figures were boosted by a strong performance from UK clothing and home furnishings.
-- UK ECONOMY CLIMBS TO SEVENTH IN WORLD

According to the World Economic Forum, a Geneva-based think tank, Britain has climbed from 15th to seventh place in a league table of the world's most competitive economies. Britain has opened up a substantial lead over European rivals, such as Germany and France and is now the envy of continental Europe. The study place Singapore in top place, followed by Hong Kong and the US.
-- SAINSBURY PICKS HOARE GOVETT AS JOINT BROKERS

Supermarket group J Sainsbury has appointed ABN AMRO Hoare Govett to act jointly with its existing stockbrokers SBC Warburg in an attempt to improve its relationship with investors following January's profit warning. This is a setback for SBC Warburg which has been the sole broker to Sainsbury since 1973. A spokesman for Sainsbury said joint brokerage is a common practice amongst FT-SE 100 companies.
THE TIMES
-- BROWN RECRUITS CBI TO UNIVERSITY OF INDUSTRY

Chancellor Gordon Brown has told the CBI about Government plans for an enterprise and growth unit within the Treasury, to be called the University of Industry, that will work with business to improve Britain's economic record. He said that partnership between British industry and the Government is crucial to the country's long-term success. He said the university will make "lifelong learning a possibility for everyone".
-- DARLING SEEKS TO CONVERT THE CITY

Chief Financial Secretary to the Treasury, Alistair Darling, is to put forward reforms of the City to the Square Mile. He says that the Treasury decided to act with a speed that has taken everyone by surprise and that details over the implementation of the new legislation need to be considered carefully. Reaction in the City has been favourable, however there is concern over how they would be policed in the future.
-- NEW DOUBTS OVER BA -AMERICAN LINK

Doubts have been raised about the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines after a meeting between the President of the Board of Trade, Margaret Beckett, and the EU competition commissioner, Karel van Miert. Beckett said the alliance raises issues which need to be addressed. The talks focussed on the Government's planned reform of competition policy in the wake of the former Director-General of Fair Trading, Lord Borrie's review.
THE GUARDIAN
-- EMU DELAY WOULD PUT 8,000 JOBS AT RISK, ROVER CLAIMS

Dr Walter Hasselkus, chairman of carmaker Rover, claims that thousands of jobs will be at risk if Britain fails to join the European single currency in the first wave. He indicated that Rover would be forced to buy many more components abroad at the cost of jobs in the UK. He also said that delay would result in an overstrong sterling exchange rate for British manufacturing and Rover would have to compensate by spending more of its budget on overseas suppliers.
-- BROWN INVITES THE NAO TO SCRUTINISE ESTIMATES

Chancellor Gordon Brown has announced that the National Audit Office, the financial watchdog for the public sector, has been invited to scrutinise the Government's estimates. He will ask the Audit Office for opinions on the assumptions underlying a range of economic estimates in an attempt to rid the annual forecasts of growth, inflation and public sector borrowing of appearing to be open to political influence.
-- POWER FIRMS ORDERED TO CUT COST OF SHOPPING AROUND

Stephen Littlechild, the electricity regulator, is set to force power companies to cut the costs of setting up computer systems for the introduction of domestic competition next year following accusations that some presented poor business plans and tried to recover costs unjustifiably. He said that the 14 regional electricity companies had estimated it would cost 850 million stg over five years to get data management systems in place.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SIB ACCUSES PRUDENTIAL OF GIVING CLIENTS WRONG ADVICE

The UK's largest insurer, Prudential, has been accused by the Securities and Investments Board, the City's main regulator, of mis-selling financial products and an alleged refusal to compensate victims. The company is accused of wrongly advising clients to place money in the Prudential Savings Account, one of its popular products, to the exclusion of more suitable investments.
-- BROWN SIGNALS OVERHAUL OF CITY REGULATIONS

Chancellor Gordon Brown has announced plans to place regulation of the entire financial services industry under one roof and remove banking supervision from the Bank of England. The move has been welcomed by the Consumers' Association who had called for the replacement of the current two-tier regulatory system with a single watchdog body. Brown outlined to the Commons plans to fold the SFA, PIA and Imro into SIB.
-- CBI WARNS OVER RAISING CORPORATE TAXES

President of the CBI, Sir Colin Marshall, has warned the Chancellor against increasing corporate taxes in his first Budget. Brown wants to raise the taxes and cut the tax credits that institutions have on dividend payments. Marshall claims this will have the long-term effect of increasing the cost of capital and force companies to top up their pension schemes from profits. He also warned the Government about upsetting the economy and criticised it over the windfall tax and its support for the Social Chapter.
